activities.anchor: comprehension had outpaced production because production demands were low
activities.caption: pair each output job with its mechanism
activities.name: sasOutputMatch

config.prompt: Output does three things input cannot — pair the job with how it works:

pairs.right: you discover you have no way to say what you mean
understanding can skate on semantics; speaking must choose forms
the correction cycle that input alone never triggers

pairs.left: retrieval at the edge of ability
pairs.right: strengthens vocabulary and grammar far more than recognition ever does

config.why: Swain's immersion children had thousands of input hours and still spoke imprecisely — the missing ingredient was being made to say it, which is also the memory science's retrieval practice.

activities.anchor: not waiting for gaps, but overlaying
activities.caption: line up the daily protocol
activities.name: sasShadowOrder

config.prompt: The shadowing protocol that works — order it, first step first:
items: Pick a 60–90 second clip of clear speech
Shadow it 5–10 times — first riding the melody, then articulating fully
Move to a new clip when it flows
config.why: One exercise, three bottlenecks stacked: articulation under time pressure, the melody layer, and real-time processing without pauses — ten to fifteen minutes daily is a complete programme.

activities.anchor: If you are waiting for the pause, you are not shadowing.
activities.caption: drag the divider — repeat, then shadow
activities.name: sasRepeatCompare

config.prompt: Two drills that look alike — drag the divider:

before.label: Listen-and-repeat
before.text: Wait for the pause, rebuild the sentence from memory — useful, and a different drill.

after.label: Shadowing
after.text: The voice rides under the speaker's as the words land, matching melody in the moment.

config.why: The simultaneity is the mechanism — that is where the articulation, prosody and processing-speed gains come from.

activities.anchor: book conversation-focused tutors and say so up front
activities.caption: call your share of the hour
activities.name: sasTalkingEstimate

config.prompt: In a well-run paid hour, how many minutes should carry YOUR voice?
config.why: About forty — the scarce resource in tutors, exchanges and meetups alike is your talking time; measure the ratio, not the price.
config.context: Tactics that raise it: agree timing splits in exchanges, topics prepared so the session never dies in logistics.

config.root: You have one paid hour and two competing goals: speed and precision.

choices.label: Free talk and description games, no interruptions
choices.feedback: Speed, courage, automaticity — and the errors go in the log for later.

choices.label: Error review and drills on yesterday's failures
choices.feedback: Precision — re-forming each error aloud, not just hearing it.

choices.label: Correct me whenever I slip, mid-flow

fluency.text: Fluency mode builds what only volume can: the courage to keep producing while the log fills.

choices.label: Schedule the review separately
choices.feedback: Two workouts, two sessions — that is the whole distinction.

accuracy.text: Accuracy work turns the log into production of the correction — precision hours are short and sharp.

choices.label: Schedule the free talk separately
choices.feedback: Neither workout substitutes for the other.

mixed.text: The every-correction session trains avoidance — the learner speaks less and less each hour.

choices.label: Re-plan the hour
choices.feedback: Pick the mode in advance; the log keeps the other goal alive.

config.why: Decide the mode in advance: talk freely now, review the noted errors at the end or in a separate session.

activities.anchor: the single best antidote to plateau despair
activities.caption: file each tactic by what it banks
activities.name: sasReadyBuckets

config.prompt: The psychological layer, made practical — file each tactic:

items.label: self-talk — narrating your day internally in the target language
repeated low-stakes attempts that train willingness to communicate
prepared fillers ("bueno, entonces…") that buy planning space
trusting that your listener's patience is higher than you model it
the monthly two-minute monologue recording on a set topic

config.why: Perfectionism schedules production after the input has already plateaued; errors with feedback are the fastest teachers — the archive shows progress the daily experience hides.

config.q: A learner logs 2,000 listening hours and still speaks haltingly. What converts understanding into producing?
choices: More of the same input — it just takes longer
Producing — a distinct stage of skill, trained only by producing
config.why: The conversion from understanding to producing is its own stage: input first and mostly, yes — input only, never.

activities.anchor: the disappearance of the translation pause before verbs
activities.caption: find the line the loyal month would love
activities.name: sasMonthSpot

config.prompt: One line of this month-plan contradicts the design — click it:
lines: Week 1: five clips from one speaker, priority on melody over articulation.
Record day 1 and day 7 doing the same clip.
Week 3: two-to-three-minute clips, plus one cold-shadow session daily.
Week 4: keep the same speaker — loyalty beats transfer.
Month-end: the two-minute monologue, compared with week 1's — pauses down, pace up.
config.correction: Switch speakers entirely — the melody habits should transfer.
config.why: If nothing moved, the clips were too hard: drop a difficulty notch and run the month again. Shadowing is measurable, which is what makes it trainable.
